title: Infrastructure Engineering Playbook: GPU Fleet, Capacity, Networking, IaC, and CI/CD
author: Asha Raman
body:
Summary:
This playbook consolidates our infra engineering standards and runbooks for GPU fleet capacity, cloud accounts and networking, Terraform/IaC modules, CI/CD pipelines and build artifacts, and operational runbooks used day-to-day by the Infra team. It is intended as the canonical reference for on-call, SRE, infra engineers, and new hires.

Audience and scope:
- Audience: infra engineers, SRE, platform engineers, and solutions engineers who operate Redwood's GPU-backed inference tier.
- Scope: Design and operational guidance for GPU fleet topology, capacity planning and autoscaling, cloud account structure and networking (VPCs, peering, routes, egress), Terraform/IaC module patterns, CI/CD best practices for infra code, and runbook procedures for common incidents.

Table of contents:
1) Principles and goals
2) Ownership and on-call responsibilities
3) GPU fleet architecture & capacity
4) Cloud accounts & networking patterns
5) Terraform / IaC module conventions
6) CI/CD and build pipelines
7) Runbooks (incidents & day-2 ops)
8) Onboarding checklist and links

1) Principles and goals
- Production-first: changes must be safe, reversible, and observable. All infra changes need automated tests + canary rollouts.
- Predictable economics: capacity and scaling decisions optimized for cost-per-token and 99.9% capacity availability for Dedicated and Private offerings.
- Separation of concerns: tenancy isolation (customer VPCs or dedicated pools) and control-plane separation for private deployments.
- Auditability and least privilege: every change is traceable and service accounts follow least-privilege principles.

2) Ownership and on-call responsibilities
- Ownership: Infra team owns GPU fleet, Terraform modules, cloud accounts, CI/CD for infra. Product/platform team own SLIs that depend on infra.
- On-call: SRE rotation covers capacity alerts and runtime incidents. Primary infra on-call is responsible for fleet scale events and emergency capacity increases.
- Escalation path: on-call -> infra lead -> platform eng mgr -> CTO on critical pager. See /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/incident-process for full escalation matrix.

3) GPU fleet architecture & capacity
Overview:
- Fleet split by workload class: interactive-low-latency, batch-high-throughput, training/ops (non-prod). Each class has separate node pools and autoscaling policies.
- Preferred hardware: NVIDIA A100 80GB or H100 (depending on region). Use Ampere SKUs in regions where quantized kernels show improved perf.
- Instance groups: use managed instance groups (cloud provider native) or EKS node groups for Kubernetes-based serving clusters.

Capacity planning targets (example):
- Target availability SLO: 99.9% of capacity requests served within 30s.
- Buffer policy: maintain a 20% warm buffer on interactive pools (i.e., reserve capacity to avoid cold-starts).
- Autoscaler thresholds: scale up when GPU utilization > 60% sustained over 2 minutes or pending queue length > 8 pods for 1 minute. Scale down when utilization < 30% for 10 minutes and buffer is satisfied.
- Scaling limits: minimum pool size = 4 GPUs for interactive pools; burst limit = configured per-customer contract.

Preemptible/spot usage:
- Use spot instances for batch workloads with checkpointing and graceful eviction handling. For interactive workloads, avoid spot unless additional fallback pools exist.
- Eviction policy: maintain 10% capacity on non-preemptible nodes as a safety pool for SLA-bound traffic.

Networking and storage considerations for GPUs:
- NVMe ephemeral disks for local KV cache; long-term model artifacts stored in object storage (S3) with lifecycle rules.
- Ensure subnets support high-bandwidth networking (ENAs or equivalent) and large MTU where supported.

Monitoring & metrics (minimum):
- Per-pool GPU utilization (1m, 5m), pod GPU memory usage, pod restart rate, pending pod queue length, model load time, inference tail latency (p95/p99).
- Alerts: GPUUtilAvg > 85% for 10m, PendingPods > 20, ModelLoadErrors increased > 5/min.

4) Cloud accounts & networking patterns
Account structure:
- Org layout: root org -> accounts: prod (redwood-prod), staging (redwood-staging), shared-services (logging, infra-tools), sandbox/dev per-team.
- Separate billing tags on capacity pools for per-customer cost allocation.

VPC and networking patterns:
- VPC per environment (prod/staging) with segmented subnets: control-plane, serving, ops, and shared services.
- Use Transit Gateway / VPC Peering for cross-account connectivity with explicit route tables.
- NAT gateways limited to a single AZ for cost; use egress NAT gateways with autoscaling for higher throughput.
- Firewalls: restrict control-plane ports; allow intra-cluster node-to-node for K8s CNI.

Private/Customer Networking:
- For Private deployments, provide reference architecture: customer-managed VPC with peering to Redwood control-plane VPC via AWS Transit Gateway or VPN. Attachment must be authorized via signed change request and an audit log entry.

Service accounts and IAM:
- Principle of least privilege: scoped roles for node provisioning, autoscaler, image pulls, metrics writing.
- Short-lived credentials using STS for automation jobs.

Network observability:
- Flow logs enabled at VPC/subnet level for prod. Centralized logging to ELK/Cloud-native equivalent for network anomalies.

5) Terraform / IaC module conventions
Module design principles:
- Modules are versioned semantically and stored in the shared modules registry (git).
- Each module must include: README, input/output schema, usage example, automated unit tests (terratest or kitchen-terraform), and changelog.
- Keep modules idempotent and design for drift detection.

Naming and layout conventions:
- Module names: cloud-provider-resource-type (e.g., aws-eks-cluster, aws-gpu-node-group, gcp-vpc).
- Root infra repo: infra-root contains environment overlays (prod/staging/share), uses module refs by version tag.

Example minimal aws-gpu-node-group usage:
```hcl
module "gpu_node_group" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood-inference/terraform-modules.git//aws-gpu-node-group?ref=v1.4.0"
  cluster_name = module.eks.cluster_name
  instance_type = "p4d.24xlarge"
  desired_capacity = 8
  min_size = 4
  max_size = 32
  labels = { pool = "interactive" }
}
```

Module lifecycle and upgrades:
- Major version upgrades must have a written upgrade plan describing impact and rollback steps.
- Use feature-flags and canary environments for module changes that touch prod clusters.

Secrets and state:
- Terraform state stored in remote state backend (S3 + DynamoDB locking for AWS). State access limited to CI roles.
- Secrets are injected at runtime from the secrets manager (SSM Parameter Store/Secrets Manager) and not checked into Git.

6) CI/CD and build pipelines
Pipeline responsibilities:
- Lint + Static analysis: terraform fmt, tflint, tfsec.
- Unit + Integration tests: terratest, kickoff harness for small infra changes.
- Plan + Apply gating: PRs must produce a terraform plan; merging to the main branch triggers a staged apply to staging then prod after approvals.

Pipeline structure for infra changes:
1. PR opened -> automated plan runs, policy checks (sentinel/tfsec) -> deploy preview to ephemeral environment (if flagged)
2. PR approvals: at least one infra reviewer and one security reviewer for changes touching IAM/networking
3. Merge -> CI run: run full test matrix -> apply to staging (auto) -> wait 24h or gated deploy window for prod and require manual approval for prod apply

Artifacts and image builds:
- Base AMIs and node images are built via Packer pipeline; images are versioned and tested in staging before promotion.
- Container images for infra components pushed to the internal registry with immutable tags (git SHA).

Policy & security gates:
- tfsec / checkov checks in PRs. Failing security checks block merge.
- Policy as Code: network and IAM policies enforced via pre-commit and CI.
- Reviewers list automatically populated for sensitive directories (iam/, network/).

Rollback and canary strategies:
- Use canary apply for changes that touch critical resources (k8s core infra, autoscaler configs). Canary target = 5% of nodes or a dedicated canary cluster.
- Rollback performed by applying previous terraform state or promoting previous artifact version; always confirm config drift is reconciled after rollback.

7) Runbooks (incidents & day-2 ops)
Runbook: High GPU pending queue (latency increase)
1. Pager fires: alert = PendingPods > 8 for > 5m or tail latency p99 > 3s for 5m.
2. On-call: verify alert in Grafana and check autoscaler logs.
3. Check recent deploys: kubectl get events, check terraform apply history in CI.
4. Immediate actions (order matters):
   a. If autoscaler failing: restart autoscaler deployment (kubectl rollout restart deployment/autoscaler) and verify logs.
   b. If autoscaler healthy but scaling blocked by quota: request temporary quota increase via cloud console and follow quota escalation template.
   c. If model load times causing backlog: redirect traffic to fallback model variant (routing in control-plane) or scale model replica count if safe.
   d. If GPU node failures: drain and replace nodes; increase desired_capacity temporarily to maintain buffer.
5. Post-incident: create incident report, record root cause, and add follow-up action item (RCA, infra change).

Runbook: Node OOM or GPU memory pressure
1. Detect: Pod OOMKilled or GPU memory usage > 95% consistently.
2. Mitigate: identify model responsible, lower max_concurrency, scale replicas horizontally if possible, or add nodes.
3. Long-term: add model-level resource limits to model onboarding checklist; instrument model memory footprints in model catalog.

Routine maintenance tasks
- Monthly: capacity review (growth rate, utilization, cost per GPU-hour).
- Quarterly: instance type review and benchmarking with representative workloads.
- Before large releases: run game-day on canary cluster to validate scale policies.

8) Onboarding checklist and links
New infra engineer checklist (first 30 days):
- Read this playbook and related runbooks.
- Get access: cloud-prod, logging, terraform state, CI credentials (request via internal portal).
- Run local terraform plan against staging overlay and familiarise with module tests.
- Join on-call shadow rotation for two weeks.

Useful links and references:
- infra-iac-and-gpu-fleet-guide-2026 (module reference)
- gpu-capacity-and-infra-runbook-2026 (incident runbook)
- infra-ci-cd-and-gpu-fleet-playbook-2026 (CI/CD examples)

Appendix: Example incident check commands
- kubectl top nodes --selector=pool=interactive
- kubectl get po -A --field-selector=status.phase=Pending
- aws autoscaling describe-auto-scaling-groups --auto-scaling-group-names <asg-name>
- terraform plan -var-file=env/staging.tfvars

Change control and approvals
- All prod-impacting changes must go through PR + code review and have at least one infra reviewer. IAM/networking changes require security reviewer approval.
- Emergency changes permitted with post-facto approvals: document reason in the PR and notify on-call and infra lead.

Maintainers and contact
- Infra engineering leads: Marco Silva (fleet & capacity), Leah Chen (cloud accounts & networking), Riley Park (IaC & CI/CD).
- Pager: infra-oncall@redwood-inference.internal

This document is reviewed quarterly and after any major incident that affects capacity or networking. For updates, edit this page and assign reviewers listed above.
